prompt: An AI invoice extractor occasionally outputs a total that doesn't match the line items. Which measure guarantees such invoices never silently reach the accounting system?

options.text: A deterministic validation step that compares totals and routes mismatches to a human
A more capable model
A prompt instructing the model to double-check its math
Temperature set to zero

explanation: Only a deterministic check catches every mismatch regardless of the model's behavior. Better models and prompts reduce error rates; validation bounds the blast radius.

prompt: Your request to an external API returns status 400. What is the correct response?

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff until it succeeds
Fix your request: a 400 means the request itself is malformed, so retries are pointless
Wait for the server to recover
Switch to a different HTTP library

explanation: 4xx errors are client errors: the request is wrong and will stay wrong on retry. Retry logic belongs to transient failures like 429 and 5xx.

prompt: Which failures deserve automatic retries with backoff?

options.text: 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden
400 Bad Request
429 Too Many Requests and 503 Service Unavailable
404 Not Found

explanation: Rate limits and server-side outages are transient: waiting and retrying (with a cap) is exactly right. Auth errors, malformed requests, and missing resources won't heal with time.

prompt: A payment API call times out and you don't know whether it was processed. The call carried an Idempotency-Key. Why is retrying now safe?

options.text: Timeouts always mean the request never arrived
The server deduplicates requests with the same key, so the charge happens at most once
The key encrypts the payment details
It isn't safe; retries of payments are always forbidden

explanation: Idempotency keys exist precisely for ambiguous outcomes: the server recognizes the repeated key and does not apply the operation twice.

prompt: Why must every production HTTP call set a timeout?

options.text: Timeouts make responses arrive faster
Without one, a hung upstream server can hang your system indefinitely
APIs reject requests that don't declare a timeout
Timeouts are only needed for file downloads

explanation: A timeout converts 'stuck forever' into a handleable error. It doesn't speed anything up: it bounds the damage when the other side misbehaves.

prompt: Which query returns cities whose average temperature since July 2026 exceeds 20°C?
code: -- table: readings(city TEXT, temp_c REAL, recorded_at TEXT)

options.text: SELECT city FROM readings WHERE AVG(temp_c) > 20 GROUP BY city
SELECT city FROM readings WHERE recorded_at >= '2026-07-01' GROUP BY city HAVING AVG(temp_c) > 20
SELECT city FROM readings HAVING temp_c > 20
SELECT AVG(city) FROM readings WHERE temp_c > 20

explanation: Row filters (the date) go in WHERE; filters on aggregated values (the average) go in HAVING after GROUP BY. Using AVG in WHERE is invalid because aggregates don't exist yet at that stage.

prompt: What makes parameterized SQL queries immune to SQL injection?

options.text: Parameters are scanned against a list of dangerous keywords
The query structure is fixed before data is bound, so user input can never be executed as SQL
Parameters are hashed before storage
The database refuses queries containing quotes

explanation: Separation of code and data: the SQL shape is compiled first and values are bound as pure data afterward. No blocklist needed: there is simply no path for data to become instructions.

prompt: Which practices belong in the handling of API keys and secrets? Select all that apply.

options.text: Store them in environment variables or a secret manager
Commit them to the repository so the team can find them
Give each key the narrowest permissions that still work
Rotate any key that was ever exposed publicly

explanation: Secrets never enter version control: Git history is forever and repos leak. Least privilege and rotation-on-exposure limit the damage when (not if) something goes wrong.

prompt: A 3-hour batch job dies at item 4,812 of 5,000 because one network call raised an uncaught exception. Which redesign fixes the actual problem?

options.text: Handle expected failures per item (retry with a limit, record, continue) and persist progress incrementally
Wrap the entire job in one try/except that ignores all errors
Run the job on a faster machine
Remove the network calls

explanation: Transient failures are expected; isolate them per item and make progress durable so a crash costs seconds. Swallowing all exceptions hides real bugs and corrupts results silently.

prompt: Why do tests of failure paths (timeouts, malformed input, duplicates) matter more than additional happy-path tests?

options.text: They run faster
Production traffic reliably contains those failure cases, and untested handling of them is where systems break
Happy-path tests are impossible to write
Failure tests are required by law

explanation: The happy path gets exercised constantly and breaks loudly in development. The failure paths run rarely, break silently, and meet real traffic: exactly where confidence is needed most.

prompt: In HTTP, which header carries a token of the form 'Bearer sk-…' to authenticate a request? (one word)
explanation: API authentication most commonly travels in the Authorization header, e.g. 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'.

prompt: Your API allows 30 requests per minute. Respecting the limit exactly, what is the minimum number of whole minutes needed to make 450 requests?
explanation: 450 ÷ 30 = 15 minutes. Rate-limit arithmetic like this decides batch job duration and whether you need to request a higher tier.

prompt: Model prompts and configuration should be version-controlled like code primarily because…

options.text: …it makes the repository look complete
…when quality shifts, you can pinpoint what changed and re-run evaluations against any past version
…prompts are too long to store in a database
…Git encrypts prompts against theft

explanation: Debugging quality regressions requires knowing exactly what changed and when. Versioned prompts + a repeatable eval suite turn a mystery into a binary search.

prompt: Why should money amounts be stored as integer cents rather than floating-point euros?

options.text: Integers use less memory
Binary floats cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly, so rounding errors accumulate in sums
Databases cannot store floats
Regulations forbid decimal points

explanation: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 in binary floating point. Financial arithmetic uses integers (or decimal types) so every cent stays exact.

prompt: In REST semantics, why should a data-fetching endpoint use GET rather than POST?

options.text: GET declares the request safe and repeatable (cacheable, retryable, and bookmarkable) while POST signals a state change
GET is faster on all networks
POST cannot return JSON
There is no difference

explanation: Verbs carry contracts: intermediaries and clients treat GET as side-effect-free. Fetching via POST forfeits caching and safe retries; mutating via GET invites disaster from prefetchers.

prompt: An API returns results in pages of 100. Your job processed page 1 and stopped. The subtle bug class this represents is…

options.text: silent partial ingestion: always follow pagination (next tokens/links) to completion and reconcile expected vs. received counts
rate limiting
a JSON syntax error
an authentication failure

explanation: Nothing errored: you just quietly got 100 of 4,000 records. Pagination handling plus count reconciliation catches what status codes can't.

prompt: A PRIMARY KEY (or UNIQUE constraint) on orders.order_id primarily buys you…

options.text: …database-enforced integrity: duplicates become impossible to insert, making the table safe to upsert against
…alphabetical ordering of rows
…automatic backups
…smaller file size

explanation: Constraints move correctness from 'code remembers to check' to 'storage refuses to be wrong': the foundation idempotent pipelines build on.

prompt: Why do small, well-described commits beat one giant 'initial commit'?

options.text: History becomes searchable and reviewable: 'what changed and why' has an answer per change, which is what debugging and code review consume
Git charges per commit size
Large commits corrupt repositories
It only matters for open source

explanation: Version control's value is the story it records. One blob commit records nothing, and reviewers (human or AI) can only review what's legible.

prompt: Configuration like API keys belongs in environment variables (or a secret store) rather than code because…

options.text: …code is shared, versioned, and long-lived while secrets must stay private and rotatable: mixing them leaks keys into Git history forever
…environment variables execute faster
…code files cannot contain strings
…it makes deployment harder, which is safer

explanation: The .env-plus-gitignore pattern separates what ships from what authenticates. Git history is effectively permanent: a committed key is a compromised key.

prompt: Your ETL script hits a record with malformed JSON in one field. Production-grade handling is to…

options.text: …catch the parse error for that record, quarantine it with context for review, count it, and continue the batch
…crash the whole batch to be safe
…silently skip it with no trace
…guess the intended value

explanation: Per-record isolation + quarantine + visibility: the batch completes, the bad record is reviewable, and the failure rate is measurable. Crash-everything and silent-skip both destroy information.
